newsitem.title: FRANCE: Giscard d'Estaing warns Paris on Maastricht target.
newsitem.headline: Giscard d'Estaing warns Paris on Maastricht target.

text.p: Former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing cautioned on Thursday that France would find it very difficult to meet European single currency criteria in late 1997 unless its economic growth quickened.

Giscard d'Estaing, who caused a stir in January by calling for a flexible interpretation of the criteria in light of an economic slowdown, ruled out any postponement of the single currency. The criteria are set out in the Maastricht treaty on European union.

"We must reach in 1997 a real growth rate above two percent," the ex-president told a lunch hosted by the Anglo-American Press Association. The government has forecast 1997 growth of 2.3 percent against 1.3 percent in 1996.

In a column for the weekly L'Express published on Thursday, the centrist Giscard d'Estaing wrote that "without stronger growth, France will have great difficulty in respecting honestly the Maastricht criteria in late 1997".

Asked whether plans for a single currency should be postponed if France or its partners failed to meet the criteria, he answered: "I believe that Germany and France will meet the criteria....The date cannot be put back because this is a very complex system."
The Maastricht Treaty calls for would-be members of a single currency to meet a range of financial critieria in 1997 in order to qualify for the final phase of monetary union in 1999.

"You'll find that several countries like Italy or Spain will be very close to the criteria. You cannot apply them to certain countries and not to others. The rule must be applied equally to all," Giscard d'Estaing said.
He also urged that the planned European Central Bank (ECB) answer to an institution other than the European Parliament.
"You mustn't confuse independence with the Bank not having to justify its policy," he said.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis has suggested a council, informally grouping ministers from countries that have joined in European monetary union after its launch in 1999, to counterbalance the ECB.

In his magazine article, the ex-president wrote that he and former West German chancellor Helmut Schmidt had set two objectives for monetary union -- to give Europe a true international currency and to give member states a solid monetary basis for durable economic growth.

"And I do not believe that our country should enter the great European monetary adventure in a weak economic and social condition," said Giscard d'Estaing, a member of the UDF, the junior partner in the ruling coalition.

Although monetary union has a serious chance of taking place and the French financial system is actively preparing to adopt the euro currency, Giscard d'Estaing said one key question remained unanswered.

"Should France enter a durable monetary system with a languid economy, company heads demoralised and demotivated by excessive charges, the risk of international takeovers of its finest industrial assets and a sadly rigid unemployment rate?" he wrote.
He also criticised the Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) on European Union institutional reform launched in Turin early this year which he said had so far yielded no result whatsoever.

He blamed a rush to announce an enlargement of the 15-member EU as soon as possible. "Only a limited degree of integration can mark this greater Europe...on which we are from now on uncautiously, but irreversibly, committed," he wrote.
